svg.title: When does an hreflang pair count?
svg.desc: Diagram of five conditions that must hold for both pages before Google uses an hreflang pair, with what happens when each fails. 1. Both pages are crawled and indexed: Annotations are picked up once all linked pages are crawled and (re)indexed. If it fails: The pair is not used until both are indexed. Hreflang does not guarantee indexing. 2. Both pages are canonical: Each canonical stays in the same language and is part of the hreflang pairs. If it fails: Hreflang is ignored. A canonical to another language can keep a version out of the index. 3. Both pages list each other, and themselves: If page X links to page Y, page Y must link back to page X. If it fails: The pair is ignored. Pairs that do link both ways still work. 4. Both codes are valid: ISO 639-1 language, optionally with an ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 region. If it fails: Region alone and codes like es-419 are not supported. Reserved codes like UK are ignored. 5. The annotations can be read and agree: Tags sit before any invalid element in the head; HTML and sitemap say the same. If it fails: Tags after an invalid head element are not read. A conflicting pair is probably dropped. Result: Google can show the version that matches the user. Same-language versions may still be folded into one canonical; hreflang may swap the URL, and reporting goes to the canonical.
svg.text: When does an hreflang pair count?
Every condition has to hold for both pages in the pair.
CONDITION
IF IT FAILS
Both pages are crawled and indexed

and (re)indexed.

language can keep a version out of the index.

If page X links to page Y, page Y must link back to page X.
The pair is ignored. Pairs that do link both ways
still work.
Both codes are valid
ISO 639-1 language, optionally with an ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2
region.
Region alone and codes like es-419 are not
supported. Reserved codes like UK are ignored.
The annotations can be read and agree
Tags sit before any invalid element in the head; HTML and
sitemap say the same.
Tags after an invalid head element are not read.
A conflicting pair is probably dropped.

Same-language versions may still be folded into one canonical; hreflang may swap the URL, and reporting goes to the
canonical.
Sources: Google Search Central documentation; statements by John Mueller (2015, 2016, 2020, 2025) and Gary Illyes (2020).
